It is also hard to outsource to a generic trust-and-safety BPO, because tone and judgment are the product.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 10-15 ex-power-mods from mod Discords and r/ModSupport who lost seats under the cap. Write a one-page playbook. Approach 30 owners of Skool communities with 1k+ paying members, using the public discovery listings. Offer a $750, 14-day pilot in which half of new joiners get the concierge and half don't. Report the day-14 retention delta and convert the best results into monthly contracts.

ideas.title: Licensed True Stories for Narration Channels
ideas.one_liner: A story studio that interviews real people about real events and licenses the recordings and scripts to faceless story-narration channels, replacing scraped Reddit posts and fake AI-written 'confessions'.
ideas.customer: Operators of faceless YouTube, TikTok and podcast channels that narrate AITA-style, revenge, workplace and relationship-drama stories, from solo operators to 10-person studios, plus audio-drama and story apps. They pay roughly $40-$150 per non-exclusive license.
ideas.problem: These channels' supply is scraped Reddit posts they don't own, since authors keep copyright and Reddit's data licenses go to AI firms, not YouTubers. YouTube's July 2025 'inauthentic content' rules specifically flag readings of material not created by the uploader and templated narrated stories, and in January 2026 YouTube terminated 16 channels with 35M combined subscribers. Mods keep banning reposts and fabricated or AI-written stories, so fresh, real material is drying up. Freelancers on Fiverr write fake 'Reddit stories' for $10-$30 that read as obvious slop.
ideas.solution: A 15-minute voice-interview app plus a human editor. The storyteller tells their story out loud, and the studio transcribes and structures it into a narration-ready script with a signed release, ID check and revenue share. Channels get a non-exclusive or exclusive license and a 'voice-verified first-person account' provenance certificate they can show as original-source proof. Authors earn a share of licensed views through tracked license codes. Storytellers are recruited off Reddit so mods aren't disrupted.
ideas.why_now: YouTube's inauthentic-content policy took effect on 15 July 2025 and was followed by the January 2026 termination wave, so channel operators now need defensible originality and provenance. At the same time AI-written fake stories have flooded the genre, and mods removing them has shrunk the pool of scrapeable real material.
ideas.revenue_model: $40-$150 per non-exclusive license, $300-$800 for exclusive first-run, and bundles such as $499 per month for 10 licenses. Authors get 40-50% of revenue. Later, sell format and option rights to audio-drama and TV producers.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Buyers are not short of scripts but of defensible originality. People tell true stories brilliantly out loud and badly in writing, so the audio-interview format both raises quality and creates a provenance signal that a text LLM can't cheaply fake. Mods know the top-performing genres and that the people who post these stories mostly do it for validation, not money, so a paid $30 interview is an easy yes.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 30 storytellers through Facebook groups, Craigslist and small creator ads at $30 per story. Produce 60 scripts with Whisper transcription plus human editing. Sell a $199 pilot pack of 10 stories to 20 narration-channel operators, found through public channel emails and faceless-creator Discords. Ask for view data on the first videos to validate the revenue-share model, and use the results as the pitch for subscription bundles.

ideas.title: Substitute-Plan Binders for Retiring Business Owners
ideas.one_liner: Retired teachers interview 60+ owner-operators and write a 'sub plan' any stranger could use to run the shop for a week, sold through business brokers.
ideas.customer: Owner-operators aged 60+ of $300k-$3M revenue businesses that depend on the owner's head (HVAC and plumbing, vet and dental practices, hardware stores, salons, daycares, landscaping). The channel and co-payer is the business broker, plus SBA lenders, CPAs and estate attorneys. Acquirers such as search-fund and ETA buyers pay later for a 'day-one' version.
ideas.problem: About 40% of small business owners are boomers, and roughly 6 million businesses will change hands by 2035. Around 70% of listed small businesses never sell, and about half of owners have no succession plan. Buyers and lenders can't underwrite what lives only in the owner's memory. Owners refuse to write SOPs, but they will talk for hours. Brokers watch listings die at the diligence stage because 'the business is the owner.'
ideas.solution: Two half-day interview sessions plus a video walk-through of the shop. Teachers are trained to draw knowledge out of people with questions. The output is a 20-40 page Sub Plan written in the classroom genre. It covers the daily schedule and routines, where the keys and passwords are, the 'kids to watch' (the difficult customer, the vendor who needs a call before noon, the employee who needs praise), emergency procedures, a first-hour and first-week script, and 'what NOT to do.' The org chart is drawn as a seating chart showing who actually influences whom. Then comes the sub test. A stranger runs a 4-hour shift from the binder, and every gap they hit gets fixed. The result becomes a diligence exhibit in the sale memorandum. AI transcription and structuring keep labor cost low, and the human elicitation stays the scarce part.
ideas.why_now: Coverage of the 'Great Ownership Transfer' peaked in 2026 (McKinsey, Forbes and others). First-time buyers via SBA 7(a) loans and search funds are flooding the market and underwriting transferability. AI transcription and structuring dropped the cost of capturing tacit knowledge by roughly 10x in the last two years. The oldest boomers turn 80 this year, and estate attorneys are seeing more 'owner died, business worthless in 90 days' cases.
ideas.revenue_model: $2,400 flat per binder, usually rolled into the broker's listing package. Brokers get a referral credit of about $300. There is a $49/month 'living binder' update plan. Buyers can pay $1,500 for a post-close rewrite. There is a $600 add-on for estate attorneys covering an 'if I'm hit by a bus' version.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The sub plan is the most battle-tested knowledge-transfer document in existence. Every teacher has written hundreds of them for a stranger with 30 unpredictable kids and six hours. No consultant has that reps count. The real asset in a small business is the informal 'kids to watch' list, which never appears in any SOP. Sellers don't fail because they lack documents. They fail because nobody asked the right questions in the right order.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 4-5 retired teachers who like interviewing. Pick one metro and pitch 20 business brokers with one offer: 'give me your stalest listing, the one that has sat 9+ months, and I'll run a free pilot binder.' Do 3 free pilots in exchange for testimonials and an intro to the broker's next 5 listings. Then charge $2,400. Add SCORE chapters, SBDCs and estate attorneys as second-wave channels.

ideas.title: Orphaned Solar Lease Cleanup at Home Closings
ideas.one_liner: A closing-desk service that untangles orphaned solar leases, PPAs and UCC fixture filings on retirees' homes so sales and estates can close.
ideas.customer: Title and escrow companies, listing agents, elder-law attorneys and estate executors, who pay per closing (fee taken from sale proceeds). Secondary customers are the retired homeowners themselves and their adult children.
ideas.problem: Door-to-door and telemarketed solar leases and PPAs were sold at kitchen tables to retirees on 20-25 year terms. Each one usually leaves a UCC-1 fixture filing on the home. The lessor may since have gone bankrupt (Sunnova filed Chapter 11 in June 2025 and its portfolio was sold and is now serviced by SunStrong; Mosaic and Sunlight failed earlier). Sales stall at the last minute because the buyer's lender wants the lease assumed or paid off and nobody can find the assignment chain, the current servicer or a payoff quote. Heirs inherit a lease on a dead parent's house, with monitoring dead and inverters failing. Homeowners rarely have copies of what they signed.
ideas.solution: A fixed-scope workflow. (1) Pull county and state fixture filings and reconstruct the chain of assignment. (2) Identify the current servicer and pull the contract. (3) Produce either a lender-ready transfer/assumption package with the buyer's credit-approval prep, or a payoff/buyout quote. (4) File the lien release. (5) Where the sales pitch looks deceptive or the lease unenforceable, hand off to a consumer attorney. A shared database of lessor entities, servicers and their turnaround times compounds as more closings run through it. The service is priced so title companies see it as saving their fee on a dying deal.
ideas.why_now: The Sunnova bankruptcy (filed June 2025, plan effective November 2025) created a live wave of stuck transfers, and multiple state AGs are investigating. The federal homeowner solar credit ended after 2025, pushing installers toward leases and PPAs, which let the company keep the tax credit. Leases signed in 2016-2020 are now reaching resale and probate age as the peak-65 cohort dies or downsizes.
ideas.revenue_model: Flat $750-$1,500 per closing, paid at settlement from proceeds. Title companies can take a $299/month priority-handling subscription. There is an optional buyout-negotiation success fee, and attorney referral fees where the state allows.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The panels are not the blocker. The blocker is paperwork nobody can find: a recorded fixture filing and an assignment chain across three companies. Closers know it as the #1 surprise at the eleventh hour. Half the street signed in 2017 with a clipboard salesman and kept no copies. Whoever owns the lessor and servicer map, and the county filing pipeline, owns the unblock.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one high-solar county in TX, FL, CA or AZ. Scrape recorded fixture filings by known lessors and cross-match them against new listings and probate filings. Call 15 title offices that have had a stuck solar closing and offer the first 3 at cost. Build template packages for the top 5 lessors and servicers. Partner with one elder-law attorney and one consumer-protection lawyer for hand-offs.

ideas.title: Pet Continuity Guarantee Funded by Shelters and Hospitals
ideas.one_liner: A membership that guarantees an older adult's pet is picked up within hours of a hospitalization and rehomed after death, paid for by the shelters and hospitals that currently absorb the cost.
ideas.customer: The payers are county animal-services agencies and shelters, hospital systems and Medicare Advantage plans, and Area Agencies on Aging. Seniors and their adult children pay a small membership.
ideas.problem: Seniors delay 911 calls, refuse admission and cut rehab short because 'nobody will feed Biscuit.' Social workers know it and nobody is paid to fix it. When the owner dies or is hospitalized long-term, the animal ends up as an owner surrender at an already crowded shelter. Nonprofit pet-guardianship programs (for example Friends of Strays) and some Meals on Wheels chapters offer emergency foster, but each is a local patchwork with no dispatch, no standard, and no way for a hospital to call at 2 a.m.
ideas.solution: Enrollment with a pet profile (vet records, medications, key-holder, behavior notes), a wallet card and a door sticker. A 24/7 dispatch line that ED nurses, discharge planners and EMS can call. A network of background-checked sitters and foster families paid per diem. A contract with a partner shelter for permanent placement, backed by a small pooled fund that acts as a pet trust in a box (roughly $1,500 per animal endowed from memberships and partner contributions). The system tracks response time and avoided surrenders, so a payer can see the return.
ideas.why_now: Shelters are running at or over capacity and paying more for intake. Hospitals are under pressure to cut ED boarding, length of stay and against-medical-advice discharges. A pet guardianship program was in the news in September 2025 (Forbes), signaling that shelters now see guardianship as core. About 4 million Americans turn 65 each year through 2027, and over half of adults 50+ own a pet (AARP).
ideas.revenue_model: B2G contract of $300-$800 per avoided surrender or per emergency placement. Hospital and health-plan fee of about $3-$6 per enrolled pet-owning member per month. Senior or family membership of $15-$25/month. Dispatch and sitter-coordination fees.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: She will never buy 'pet insurance.' She thinks of it as 'who takes Biscuit.' The barrier to care is emotional and logistical, and hospitals and shelters both pay for the consequences without seeing the link. Existing guardianship programs are capped not by adopters but by the lack of a 4-hour dispatch and response system.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign one county shelter and one hospital ED or social-work team as pilot partners. Enroll 50 seniors through Meals on Wheels routes and senior centers. Recruit 15 sitters from local sitter platforms with background checks. Track hours to placement and avoided surrenders, and use the numbers to close the first paid contract.

ideas.title: The Weekly Mail Box for Mom
ideas.one_liner: A prepaid return envelope where a parent drops all her mail. It gets scanned, triaged, shredded, and turned into a 'what needs doing' digest for her adult child.
ideas.customer: Adult children aged 45-62 with a parent 75+ living alone, often 100+ miles away. Secondary customers are daily money managers, professional fiduciaries and elder-law firms who currently collect and read mail by hand.
ideas.problem: Paper mail is where scams (fake invoices, 'prize fees', Medicare plan pitches), real bills and the notices that cost money arrive: property-tax exemption renewals, Part D changes, IRS notices, Medicaid paperwork. Kids discover the unopened shoebox at Thanksgiving. USPS Informed Delivery shows only the exterior of some letter-size mail. Parents refuse apps, dashboards and shared passwords because that feels like surrender.
ideas.solution: A weekly pre-addressed return flat that the parent fills with the whole pile, with no sorting. The team scans it, uses AI to classify and extract sender, amount, due date and required action, flags likely scams (any 'send a check to claim your prize' letter), and calls or texts the parent for urgent items ('Do you want the water bill paid?'). The child gets a weekly digest and a dashboard. Originals are shredded or returned monthly, per the parent's choice. Over time it builds the 'where everything is' paper trail that estates need: accounts, policies, pensions and annuities.
ideas.why_now: Cheap, accurate AI document extraction only became affordable at consumer prices in the last two years. Treasury phased out paper checks on Sept 30, 2025, and agencies are pushing digital, while seniors still get paper notices. Older-adult scam losses run in the billions per year (FTC). Medicare open enrollment begins Oct 15, so the mailer flood is imminent.
ideas.revenue_model: $49/month per household (about $14 in postage, scanning and AI, for roughly 70% gross margin). $25 per household per month wholesale for daily money managers and fiduciaries. Optional $149 one-time 'estate paper trail' report.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Seniors will turn down every dashboard, but they will hand over an envelope pile happily, because mailing is a ritual they own. The pile is the real system of record for a widow's finances. Scam checks and wire requests are usually triggered by letters, so scanning the inside of the envelope catches what exterior-only tools cannot. Children do not want passwords either. They want to know what to pay.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 30 households in one metro through caregiver Facebook groups, local AARP caregiver meetings and elder-law attorneys. Run it manually with a $500 duplex scanner, an AI extraction pipeline and a retired teacher doing quality checks. Charge from day one. Track 'catches' (scams intercepted, missed notices found) and publish them. Then pitch daily money managers.

ideas.title: Church-Basement Microschools for Retired Teachers
ideas.one_liner: A turnkey venue, insurance, fire-code and ESA-billing kit that lets a retired teacher open an 8-15 student paid school in a congregation's empty weekday classrooms.
ideas.customer: Retired or soon-to-retire teachers aged 55-70 pay a monthly fee and a share of tuition. Congregations are the landlords. Parents are the end payers, through education savings account (ESA) funds.
ideas.problem: Microschool builders assume curriculum and tech are the hard part. What actually kills these schools is the certificate of occupancy and zoning, the fire marshal, liability insurance, ESA vendor approval and reimbursement paperwork, and bookkeeping. Retired teachers have the credibility and skills but no business experience. Meanwhile congregations hold Sunday-school classrooms that sit empty Monday to Friday and need rent.
ideas.solution: A state-by-state permit packet (occupancy class, what the inspector will actually ask for). A pre-negotiated group liability policy for microschools. A standard five-day lease with congregations covering rent, cleaning, security and safeguarding. Onboarding for ESA and voucher programs (including any accreditation or approved-provider requirements) plus back-office billing and attendance. A menu of curricula so the teacher chooses. A shared bench of substitute retired teachers for sick days.
ideas.why_now: Texas launched its Education Freedom Accounts in fall 2026 with $1 billion, about $10,474 per student in 2026-27 (a 12-student school is roughly $125k in revenue), and about 600 private schools and pre-K providers applied in the first 10 days. Universal or near-universal ESAs are live in a growing list of states, and a federal scholarship tax credit begins in 2027. About 1.5 million students are already in microschools, and teacher retirements are climbing.
ideas.revenue_model: $199-$399/month platform fee per school, about 4% of tuition processed, insurance commissions, and a 5% lease-admin fee from congregations.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Pension re-employment caps generally bite when you return to a covered public district. Working for yourself in a private school usually does not touch your annuity (verify by state), and past full retirement age the Social Security earnings test no longer applies. So a retired teacher can keep her pension and collect full tuition. Parents' top trust signal is 'Mrs. Alvarez taught 31 years at Lincoln Elementary.' A church building that is already zoned, already inspected for children, and rents for $800-$1,500 a month is the cost moat. Curriculum is commodity. Occupancy and insurance are the moat.
ideas.first_30_days: In Texas or Arizona or Florida, recruit a cohort of 10 retired teachers through retired-educator associations and Facebook groups. Line up 5 congregations with weekday space. Build the permit checklist for one city, get one group insurance quote, and sign 3 pilot schools at $299/month. Target the January 2027 semester and the early-2027 ESA application cycle for 2027-28, since fall 2026 enrollment has already closed.

ideas.title: Supplier Divorce Protection: Tool Census and Overrun Forensics
ideas.one_liner: When a US manufacturer leaves a Chinese contract manufacturer, we find out which molds and dies it really owns, and prove whether the ex-supplier is still running them off the books.
ideas.customer: US OEMs and PE-owned manufacturers ($50M-$500M revenue) that moved or are moving injection-molded, die-cast, stamped or extruded product out of China within the last 24 months, and hold $200k-$5M of tooling there. The buyer is the COO or VP Supply Chain, with General Counsel as co-signer. General counsel and brand-protection managers are the second buyer.
ideas.problem: Most small and mid-size OEMs cannot say which tools they own, where they physically sit, or what condition they are in. The paper trail is a PO line item from 2016 and a WeChat thread. When the relationship ends, the supplier slow-walks tool release, demands storage or release fees, and sometimes runs overruns on your tooling on a third shift and sells them to distributors and marketplaces at a discount. You then compete against your own product, and lawyers cannot help because nobody can prove which tool made which part.
ideas.solution: Three stacked products. (1) Tool Census: a local partner audits each supplier on video and in person, laser-tags every tool with a serial, records its condition and appraised value, and captures a macro-photo 'fingerprint' library of each cavity (gate vestige, ejector-pin witness marks, texture flaws, parting-line signature). (2) Overrun Watch: monitor Amazon, Alibaba, 1688, Temu, eBay and Walmart Marketplace for look-alike parts, buy samples, and match them to cavity fingerprints, date wheels and lot codes with computer-vision-assisted forensics. That yields evidence packs for marketplace takedowns, CBP IPR recordation, or counsel. (3) Tool Extraction: negotiate release, handle Chinese export paperwork and freight, and re-qualify the tool in Ohio.
ideas.why_now: The Reshoring Initiative's 2026 survey shows 36% of OEMs reshored this year, up from 29%. The 2025 tariff whiplash ended a lot of Chinese supplier relationships, and the Feb 2026 Supreme Court IEEPA ruling is now churning sourcing decisions again, so the number of messy breakups is at a peak. Cheap macro-imaging and vision models make tool-mark matching, previously an expensive forensic-lab exercise, feasible at SMB prices.
ideas.revenue_model: Tool Census at $6k-$15k per supplier site. Overrun Watch at $2k-$5k per month per product family. Forensic evidence pack at $3k-$8k per case. Extraction at 8-12% of appraised tool value plus pass-through freight. Expected first-year ACV per client is $40k-$120k.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Outsiders think IP loss in China means someone copies your design. Insiders know the far bigger leak is your own paid-for tool running unrecorded shifts, and that every cavity is a physical fingerprint the supplier cannot deny. Ownership of the tooling is the real leverage in any break-up, and almost nobody documents it until the day they need it.
ideas.first_30_days: Skip China operations at first. Sell a remote $2,500 'Marketplace Overrun Audit': buy 10 units of the client's product from 1688, Alibaba and Temu, compare them to the golden sample and lot codes, and deliver a one-page verdict. Sign 3 design partners through Ohio plant-manager and Reshoring Initiative networks, and line up a Dongguan or Ningbo audit contractor by referral. Book a one-hour consult with an IP litigator who will white-label the evidence-pack format.

ideas.title: Power Passport: Scoring Dead Factories on Amps, Permits
ideas.one_liner: A database and paid inspection report that rates shuttered Midwest plants on the things reshoring manufacturers actually need (utility service, slab, crane, transferable air and discharge permits) instead of square footage.
ideas.customer: Reshoring manufacturers and their site-selection consultants (first buyer). Industrial listing brokers and sellers of dead factories (they pay to differentiate their listings). Regional economic-development bodies and utility economic-development teams (annual license).
ideas.problem: Brokers list buildings by square feet, clear height and dock doors. A reshoring plant needs enough energized 480V/13.2kV capacity, a slab that can carry presses and large CNCs, crane rails, and a transferable Ohio EPA air permit for a paint or wash line. Greenfield permitting and long-lead transformers and switchgear can add 9-18 months before the first good part. Meanwhile data-center developers are hunting the same brownfield shells for their existing utility service, so the buildings that suit manufacturing are disappearing without either side understanding what was in them.
ideas.solution: Build a parcel-level dataset of pre-2005 industrial buildings across Ohio, Pennsylvania, Michigan and Indiana by combining public air and wastewater permit records, county parcel data, utility maps, aerial imagery for crane bays and rail spurs, and Phase I history. Score each building on power, permits, structure and contamination risk. Sell a 'Power Passport': a 12-page report with a licensed industrial electrician's walk-through, gear nameplate photos, permit transferability notes and utility will-serve context, delivered in 5 days.
ideas.why_now: The 2026 reshoring wave and the data-center land grab are competing for the same shells. Transformer and switchgear lead times are still measured in many months to years. The gap between what manufacturers need and what listings say is at its widest, and brokers have no tooling to fill it.
ideas.revenue_model: $1.5k-$3.5k per Passport (paid by the broker or seller, or by the buyer). A 0.5%-1% success fee on closed industrial deals. $25k-$60k per year data licences to economic-development agencies, utilities and site-selection firms. Later, a capital vehicle that buys the best shells and subdivides them into permitted multi-tenant 'factory condos'.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In a dead Ohio plant the building is the cheapest part. The energized service, the paper permits and the crane rails are the asset, and they are invisible to anyone who has not tried to open a factory. Every reshorer I know lost most of a year to power and permits, not to hiring.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one metro (Akron/Canton or the Mahoning Valley). Pull public Ohio EPA permit records and county parcel data to list 150 candidate buildings. Hire an electrician for 20 walk-throughs at about $150 per hour. Cold-call 25 industrial listing brokers offering a free first Passport in exchange for a testimonial and a right to the data. Convert 3-5 into paying $1.5k reports and one economic-development office into a pilot licence.

ideas.title: Finishing Milk Run for Small Machine Shops
ideas.one_liner: A scheduled truck route and capacity-slot exchange that pools small lots from many shops into full tank loads and racks at platers, anodizers, heat treaters and powder coaters.
ideas.customer: Job shops and small OEM plants (5-150 employees) that machine or fabricate parts but outsource plating, anodize, passivation, heat treat, e-coat or powder coat. The buyer is the shop owner or plant manager. The second customer is the finisher, who gets fuller tanks and lines.
ideas.problem: Everyone talks about a shortage of machinists, but the real reshoring bottleneck is finishing. Parts wait 9-15 days for a truck and for enough volume to fill a tank or rack. Finishers apply minimum-charge lots that punish small runs. Shops drive parts themselves or pay LTL rates of $150-$300 per pallet, and a batch's lead time is mostly waiting, not processing. The 2026 Reshoring Initiative data show finishing capacity as part of the bottleneck, and permits make new capacity slow and rare.
ideas.solution: Run daily box-truck routes around a dense corridor (Akron-Canton-Cleveland-Youngstown) with QR-coded totes and text-message status. Pre-buy weekly capacity slots at 8-12 vetted finishers, pool many shops' small lots into shared racks, and guarantee 3-5 day door-to-door turnaround. Route data and slot utilisation decide which finisher gets which parts. Expand to a second corridor (Columbus-Dayton-Cincinnati) once route density works.
ideas.why_now: Reshoring is adding machined and fabricated volume in the US while environmental permits have made new plating, anodize and coating lines almost impossible to build. Existing finishers are running full but inefficiently. Lightweight route and tote software plus cheap dispatch tools remove the reason this stayed a hand-arranged, phone-call business.
ideas.revenue_model: $55-$95 per stop or tote pickup, an 8-12% margin on capacity-slot resale, and a $299/month booking and tracking subscription. Roughly 40 active shops on one corridor gets to $1M ARR. Later, purchase or co-develop a permitted finishing line inside a 'factory condo'.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: An anodize or zinc cycle takes hours. Most of the lead time is a batch waiting for a truck and waiting for enough peers to fill a rack. That is a logistics-and-pooling problem hiding inside what everyone treats as a process-capacity problem, and it is solvable without building a single tank.
ideas.first_30_days: Lease one box truck or contract a local courier per stop. Interview 15 shops and 4 finishers. Launch one route on Tuesdays and Thursdays with 8 pilot shops at $65 per stop. Get two finishers to guarantee 48-hour processing for pooled lots in exchange for weekly committed volume. Track everything in Airtable with printed QR tags and text updates, and publish on-time-in-full data after 6 weeks.

ideas.title: Tariff Surcharge Credit-Memo Recovery for Mid-Size Manufacturers
ideas.one_liner: Mine a plant's accounts-payable history for 2025-26 tariff surcharges, then win credit memos from the distributors who are now receiving IEEPA refunds.
ideas.customer: US manufacturers with $5M-$200M revenue and 30-300 active vendors who paid line-item 'tariff surcharges' or tariff-justified price increases from March 2025 through the February 2026 Supreme Court ruling. The buyer is the CFO, controller or purchasing director.
ideas.problem: Refunds go to the importer of record, and importers of record are usually distributors: fastener houses, bearing and fitting suppliers, steel service centers, electronics distributors, tooling vendors. The plant paid the surcharge but has no claim with CBP. Downstream buyers have to rely on contract and unjust-enrichment theories against the vendor. Large retailers have law firms doing this, but a $4k-$60k claim per vendor is below any law firm's floor. Plant managers also will not sue the only source of a hydraulic fitting, so the claims are simply going unasked.
ideas.solution: 'SurchargeScan': connect to QuickBooks, NetSuite, Epicor or Infor (or upload AP PDFs). AI extracts surcharge lines and tariff-justified price-increase letters, ranks vendors by likelihood of being the importer of record (using public bill-of-lading data and vendor type), and generates reservation-of-rights letters. It then runs a relationship-preserving negotiation for credit memos against future orders instead of cash demands, and tracks each vendor's refund status through CBP's CAPE process. A partner law firm signs off on letters and escalates only large or hostile cases.
ideas.why_now: The Supreme Court held the IEEPA tariffs unlawful in February 2026. CBP launched its CAPE refund module on April 20, 2026, with well over $100B accepted for processing. The government is appealing the Court of International Trade's refund order, so vendors are receiving cash now while uncertainty still gives buyers leverage. Every month vendors book the windfall as profit, the claim gets harder to recover.
ideas.revenue_model: 20%-25% contingency on recovered credits and cash, plus a $499 scan fee credited against the fee. Average expected recovery of $25k-$150k per plant, with margins on a heavily automated flow. Later, an ongoing 'duty-pass-through audit' for any future tariff regime.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Nobody in the surcharge fight wants to be in court with their own supplier. Plant managers will happily take a credit memo on the next PO but will never file a lawsuit, so the winning product is a diplomatic credit negotiation run by software, not a demand-letter factory.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 5 Ohio plant controllers as design partners with a free scan in return for 20% on recoveries. Build the scanner with an LLM over exported AP data plus a public bill-of-lading lookup. Send 20 reservation-of-rights letters and get the first credit memos booked. Sign a referral and review agreement with one trade-law boutique. Publish the recovery rate data from the first 10 vendors to sell the next 50 plants.

ideas.title: Assay-Verified Swarf Pooling for Machine Shops
ideas.one_liner: Turn the chip bin into a revenue line: two-bin alloy segregation, assayed weekly pickup, and pooled truckloads sold direct to mills and remelters.
ideas.customer: Ohio job shops and mid-size plants (20-300 employees) machining stainless, nickel alloys, titanium, brass or tool steel, especially aerospace, energy and medical suppliers. The first buyer is the plant manager or owner. A second buyer is any prime or OEM that wants a closed-loop 'revert' chain-of-custody.
ideas.problem: The chip bin is the only place in a shop where money leaves blind. Most shops tip all chips into one roll-off. The scrap yard grades by eye or its own XRF and pays a mixed-lot price. One shovel of aluminum in 316 stainless, or too much cutting oil, can drop the price by 30%-70%, while clean, segregated titanium and nickel-alloy turnings sell at multiples of mixed scrap. Nobody at the shop has time to sort, and small volumes are too tiny for mills to accept directly.
ideas.solution: 'SwarfStack': color-coded, RFID-tagged two- and three-bin systems in the shop, plus a weekly route truck with an onboard scale and a handheld XRF that assays each pickup and logs photo, weight, alloy and oil content to a shared ledger. A centrifuge or briquetter handles the oil. Pool by alloy across dozens of shops into full truckloads sold directly to mills, foundries and remelters. Pay the shop 70%-80% of net price and issue a digital scrap certificate for chain-of-custody. The provenance data becomes more valuable as metals tariffs increasingly reward proof of where metal was melted.
ideas.why_now: Reshoring is adding domestic machining hours, and with them chips. Metals lead times and alloy volatility keep prices high. The April 2026 Section 232 rewrite taxes the full customs value of metal derivatives and gives better treatment to U.S.-melted content, so provenance now has a price. Used handheld XRF analyzers now cost about what a used pickup does, and cheap vision models can identify alloy family from a photo of a bin.
ideas.revenue_model: A 20%-30% spread between the pooled sale price and what the shop is paid, plus $150-$300 per month bin and route fees, plus a small fee per digital scrap certificate. A route with 60 shops averaging $1,500 per month of chip value nets about $250k-$400k per year, before adding a briquetting and coolant-recovery arm.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The scrap dealer's edge is not market power, it is that the shop does not know what is in its own bin. The metal was worth far more than the 'mixed' price, and shops give away five-figure sums each year without ever seeing the invoice line.
ideas.first_30_days: Buy a used handheld XRF for about $15k-$25k and rent a pickup with a platform scale. Sign 8 aerospace and medical suppliers in one county, starting with those cutting titanium, Inconel or stainless. Run pickups, assay each load, and send each shop a 'you left $X in your bin' statement showing the uplift against their current dealer. Pre-sell pooled loads to one stainless remelter and one titanium remelter before the first truckload.

ideas.title: Pre-Registered Neighbor Impact Studies for Data Centers
ideas.one_liner: A neutral 'testing lab' for whether a data center, battery plant or transmission line lowers nearby home values, with the method locked and published before anyone sees the results.
ideas.customer: Four payers. (1) Data center, BESS, solar and transmission developers facing moratoria or rezoning hearings pay $15-60k per study. (2) County and city planning departments and utility commissions pay $10-40k for a neutral study. (3) Resident coalitions and HOAs pay $3-8k for a 'lite' study, usually crowdfunded. (4) Landowner condemnation and easement attorneys.
ideas.problem: Every land-use fight ends in dueling consultant reports. Developer studies use hand-picked matched pairs that always show 'no impact'. Residents bring anecdotes. Planning staff can't judge either side, so boards vote on vibes and moratoria spread. Nobody trusts any report, so the reports are worthless.
ideas.solution: A repeatable, pre-registered protocol. Step 1: publish (timestamped and hashed) the analysis plan, including radius bands, event dates and exclusion rules. Step 2: pull every arm's-length sale within 0.25 to 2 miles, before and after the announcement date and the operation date. Step 3: run a repeat-sales difference-in-differences or synthetic-control analysis against similar areas that had no project. Step 4: have a licensed appraiser review every sale for arm's-length status, condition and segment (estates, REO and investor flips get pulled), and do a ground visit for what is actually audible and visible from the homes. Step 5: deliver a USPAP-compliant consulting report plus an interactive map. Results are published whichever way they come out. Add a 5-year 'impact monitor' subscription for counties and developers that tracks post-operation sales.
ideas.why_now: AI-driven data center siting in 2025-26 has produced local moratoria, rezoning denials and noise complaints in many states (VA, GA, TX, AZ, IN, OH). Property values are one of the top arguments alongside power and water. Federal and state pushes to speed up transmission and energy siting mean more condemnation and easement fights. Public sales data plus cheap compute make a rigorous study a $10k job instead of a $100k one.
ideas.revenue_model: Fixed-fee studies, paid upfront into escrow so the client cannot steer the result. Annual retainers for repeat developers (for example 8-10 sites a year). $10-15k/yr monitoring subscriptions for counties. Later, an 'Impact Study Standard' certification that planning codes can reference.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Appraisers know matched-pair studies are the hired gun's favorite toy: pick 6 pairs that support the client and you're done, and both sides know it. Credibility is the scarce input, not analysis. Pre-registration is standard in clinical trials and unheard of in appraisal. Developers will pay for a study that might go against them, because a study nobody believes is worth nothing at a hearing. The other secret is timing. Buyer perception moves at announcement, before the first shovel, so studies run only on 'after operation' miss the effect. A difference-in-differences on the announcement date catches it.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one hot metro (for example Northern Virginia or metro Atlanta). Run a free 'shadow study' on existing data centers there using public sales records, with the method pre-registered on a public page. Email planning directors, 10 resident groups and 5 developer permitting leads. Recruit two appraisers as signing reviewers. Aim to sign one $12-20k study, or a county pilot, by day 30-45.

ideas.title: Private Road Agreements That Save Rural Closings
ideas.one_liner: A flat-fee e-sign-and-record service that produces the road-maintenance and shared-well agreements lenders demand, then turns each road into a dues-collecting association.
ideas.customer: Listing and buyer agents and title/escrow officers in rural and mountain markets (CO, MT, ID, WA, OR, UT, NC/TN mountains, northern New England) pay $400-750 per transaction. Later, the households on each road pay $15-40 a month through the association.
ideas.problem: A house on a private road often has no enforceable maintenance agreement, only a handshake among neighbors. FHA, VA, USDA and most conventional underwriters want a recorded, legally enforceable agreement, and similar paper for shared wells, septics and driveways. The appraiser flags the private road and the problem lands on nobody. It surfaces 7-10 days before closing, the neighbors have no reason to cooperate, and the deal slips or dies. Between sales the road decays because nobody can collect dues.
ideas.solution: Software plus templated law. (1) Detect private vs public roads from county GIS and identify every benefiting parcel and owner. (2) Use state-specific agreement templates reviewed once by local counsel. (3) Run a multi-party e-sign, remote online notarization and e-recording workflow with a friendly neighbor-outreach script. (4) Add a lender-ready cover letter that answers the standard underwriting condition. (5) Upsell to a formal road association (entity, EIN, bank account, ACH dues billing, reserve tracking, lien rights where state statute allows) and shared well/septic agreements.
ideas.why_now: Affordability pushes buyers toward exurban and rural homes, and many of them rely on FHA, VA or USDA financing with strict access rules. Remote online notarization and e-recording are now legal and routine in most states. Counties are refusing to accept new roads into public maintenance. Wildfire-zone insurers and fire districts increasingly care about year-round road access and maintenance.
ideas.revenue_model: $495 flat per agreement package, paid by the seller through escrow or by a title partner, plus pass-through recording fees. $250 add-on per shared well, septic or easement agreement. Recurring: $29/month association software plus a payment fee on dues (about 3% + $3 per household per month). Referral fees from title partners.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The road is not the deal-killer. The 4-30 neighbors who each have zero incentive to sign are. So the product is the neighbor-consent workflow, not the document. The other insider fact is that underwriters usually accept a simple recorded agreement signed by a majority of owners with proportional cost shares. You don't need a full HOA. Once a road has bank-account-backed dues, it becomes a sticky recurring customer that nobody else serves.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick 2 counties dense with private roads (for example the foothills of Larimer/Boulder CO, or Flathead MT). Pull active listings and cross-match them to county road-class GIS to find listings on private roads. Pay a local real-estate attorney about $2-3k to review one template. Cold-contact those listing agents with a specific message: your listing is on a private road, the lender will ask for this, and we deliver in 7 days. Sign 5 pilots at $495 and 2 title officers as referral partners.

ideas.title: Pre-Loss Home Reconstruction Dossiers for Insurance Claims
ideas.one_liner: Rebuild, in the exact quality and condition language insurers can't wave away, what a destroyed home actually had, using old appraisals, listing photos, permits and imagery.
ideas.customer: Public adjusters and policyholder-side insurance attorneys handling total-loss wildfire, hurricane and tornado claims pay $900-2,500 per dossier. Direct-to-homeowner is $495 for a basic version. Independent insurance agents later buy a 'pre-loss baseline' for their high-value clients.
ideas.problem: After a total loss, the insurer's estimate assumes builder-grade finishes and smaller square footage. The survivor's photos and receipts burned, so 'like kind and quality' becomes a memory-versus-spreadsheet fight worth tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars per house. Public adjusters reconstruct from Zillow photos and homeowner recollection, which adjusters on the other side discount.
ideas.solution: A retrospective, signed 'as-was' dossier delivered in about 5 business days. Sources: (1) any prior purchase or refinance appraisal the homeowner has (borrowers are entitled to copies) or can get through the lender or servicer; (2) archived MLS photos and remarks from the last sale; (3) permit and remodel history; (4) assessor quality and size records; (5) historical aerial and street-level imagery. A licensed appraiser assigns the standard Q1-Q6 quality and C1-C6 condition ratings, lists the finishes and features, and estimates replacement cost at that quality level.
ideas.why_now: The January 2025 Los Angeles fires destroyed roughly 16,000 structures, and many claims are still being contested in late 2026. Every wildfire and hurricane season adds more total losses. Insurers are tightening costs and leaning on adjuster software. Photo and record archives from prior sales are now digital and searchable, so the reconstruction is a 5-day job.
ideas.revenue_model: Flat fee per dossier only. USPAP forbids contingent appraisal fees, and independence is the product's credibility. Volume pricing for public adjuster firms. $99/yr 'baseline vault' (current LiDAR, photos and Q/C ratings) sold through independent insurance agents in wildfire and hurricane zones, who carry E&O exposure when clients are underinsured.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The best pre-loss evidence in America already exists, sitting in lender closing files, appraisal workfiles kept five years and old MLS pages. Nobody connects it to claims. A neutral licensed appraiser's dated interior photos and Q/C ratings carry far more weight with an insurer than a homeowner's testimony. Those disputes are won at the finish level (cabinetry, flooring, millwork), not on square footage, and the appraiser's rating vocabulary is what claims examiners recognize.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 3 appraisers in Los Angeles County who lost work. Build one dossier template. Offer 5 free pilot dossiers to 2-3 public adjuster firms and one policyholder attorney working Altadena or Pacific Palisades cases, and measure how much the insurer's revised offer moves. Then charge $1,500 per dossier and use the measured lift as the sales pitch.

ideas.title: Builder Defect Outbreak Radar From Permit Clusters
ideas.one_liner: Epidemiology for houses: read repair-permit clusters by builder, subdivision and vintage to tell HOA boards they have a defect outbreak and how many months remain on the legal clock.
ideas.customer: HOA management companies and reserve-study firms (about $99-250 per community per year, or a $750 one-time scan). Independent home inspectors and buyer's agents in new-build subdivisions ($19-39 per address). Later, home-warranty companies and homeowners insurers as data licensees.
ideas.problem: Production-home defects (roofs, windows, stucco or siding, plumbing, foundations) show up as patterns, but each owner sees only their own house. Boards learn late. Statutes of repose and limitation for construction-defect claims typically run roughly 6-10 years depending on state and quietly expire. Buyers pay for the defect discount without knowing why, and the MLS says nothing.
ideas.solution: Ingest city and county permit data. Use an LLM to classify messy permit text (re-roof, window replacement, siding or stucco remediation, re-pipe, foundation or pier repair, water-intrusion repair). Tie parcels to subdivision, builder and year built from plat and assessor data. Compare repair-permit rates to age-matched control cohorts in the same metro. Flag statistically significant outliers. Deliver a 'Community Defect Scan': map, cohort comparison, estimated time left under the applicable state statute (information, not legal advice), and next steps (independent engineer, reserve study update, attorney consult). Also offer a per-address flag API for inspectors.
ideas.why_now: The 2020-2022 building boom, built under labor and material shortages with substitutions, is now 4-6 years old, when defects surface and the earliest repose clocks start closing. Permit portals and open data are far more digitized than five years ago. LLMs make classification of messy permit text nearly free. Insurers and lenders are increasingly sensitive to new-build condition.
ideas.revenue_model: Community scans at $750 one-time. Management-company portfolio subscriptions at $99-250 per community per year. Per-address inspector add-on at $19-39. Data licensing to warranty and insurance underwriters. Flat fees only, with no referral fees to law firms, to avoid fee-splitting problems.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Individual defects are invisible, but outbreaks are not. Appraisers watch this pattern for years without a feed: neighbors all re-roofing in year 5, three permits for the same water-intrusion fix on one street. The payer isn't the buyer, it's the board with a ticking legal deadline and a manager who wants to look proactive. The trick that makes a 'builder X is an outlier' claim defensible is controlling for age, since old-house repairs are normal and only age-matched cohort comparison isolates the builder.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one metro with clean open permit data and heavy 2019-22 production building (for example Denver suburbs, Phoenix East Valley or Austin/Round Rock). Build the pipeline over about 200 subdivisions. Produce 10 free scans for community managers. Have counsel review the wording (state permit counts and method only, no accusations). Pitch 5 management companies and 3 reserve-study firms, and sell the first 10 scans at $750.

ideas.title: Retirement-in-a-Box for Exiting Appraisers
ideas.one_liner: Take the workfile custody, E&O tail worry and direct lender clients off retiring appraisers, then hand the practice to supervised trainees, a bridge the industry has never had.
ideas.customer: Certified residential appraisers about 58 and older deciding whether to learn the new UAD 3.6 workflow or quit pay $1,500-2,500 one-time. Successor side: credit unions, community banks and attorneys with direct-relationship orders pay recurring fees. Career-changers (agents, inspectors, adjusters, contractors) become trainees under our supervisors.
ideas.problem: An appraisal practice has no sale value. The license is personal and the AMC clients aren't transferable. Retirement is also frightening. USPAP requires workfiles to be retained and retrievable for at least 5 years (longer with litigation). E&O claims can arrive years later, so a costly tail policy is needed. Board complaints and subpoenas don't stop. Meanwhile UAD 3.6 becomes mandatory Nov 2, 2026 with new forms and data, which is pushing veterans to quit rather than relearn. The active workforce has reportedly shrunk from over 90,000 (2016) to about 65,000, and rural counties lose their only appraiser.
ideas.solution: (1) Secure digital workfile custody with retrieval, subpoena and board-inquiry response, and a group E&O tail program (brokerage commission). (2) A recorded 3-hour 'local knowledge' interview plus the retiree's adjustment grids and neighborhood boundary notes, packaged into a playbook for the successor. (3) Successor placement: trainees under a certified supervisor of record (the retiree part-time for 12-24 months on a stipend and earn-out, or another certified appraiser), with desk-review and AI QC before signature. (4) The retiree's direct lender clients move to the successor with a personal handoff.
ideas.why_now: UAD 3.6 is mandatory for new GSE submissions from Nov 2, 2026. The AQB's second exposure draft (comments closed Aug 30, 2026) proposes removing the college-degree requirement and experience-timeline barriers, which widens the trainee pool. Executive Order 14393 (March 2026) directs regulators to simplify appraiser qualifications and expand alternative valuations. The rural shortage is acute and lenders want reliable local coverage.
ideas.revenue_model: $1,800 one-time custody plus transition package, or about $29/month for archive-only. E&O tail brokerage commissions. A 15-25% earn-out on inherited direct-client revenue for 24 months. 20-30% of trainee-produced fee revenue for QC and supervisor-of-record services. Coverage-guarantee contracts with rural credit unions and community banks.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The asset isn't the license. It's about 200 workfiles, 15 direct-client phone numbers and 25 years of local adjustment knowledge, and the real exit barrier is fear of tail liability, not money. Solve the fear and the successor gets clients and know-how at near-zero acquisition cost. VCs assume AI will make appraisers obsolete. The near-term truth is that the supply of human signatures (the liability bearers) is collapsing faster than software replaces them, and whoever owns the signatures and the QC owns the workflow. Supervisors, not trainees, are the scarce resource.
ideas.first_30_days: Pull public state board rosters in 3-4 states (for example TX, OH, PA, CO) and filter certified residential appraisers licensed 25+ years. Run a free 'UAD 3.6: adapt or retire' session through local Appraisal Institute chapters and appraiser Facebook groups. Sign 10 retirees to the $1,500 custody plus tail package. Recruit 5 trainees from local agents and inspectors. Hold two credit union lunches to line up the direct-client handoffs.

ideas.title: Dead Capital: Succession Kits for Diaspora Families
ideas.one_liner: A flat-fee, advocate-supervised 'estate file' service that gets a dead parent's or grandfather's land, shares and dormant accounts legally transferred, sold to the adult children who pay from Nairobi, Dallas or Dubai.
ideas.customer: Salaried urban and diaspora Kenyans aged 30-55 whose rural parents or grandparents died (or are old) with land still registered in a dead person's name. They pay from abroad or from the city. A secondary B2B payer is any SACCO, coop or bank that needs cleared successions before it releases deposits or lends against land.
ideas.problem: Most rural family land is still titled to a dead grandfather or father because nobody completed succession. The process needs a chief's letter, a death certificate, consents from every heir, gazettement, a wait before confirmation of grant, and then transmission at the land registry, which is often 1-3 years and many trips. Until it is done the land cannot be leased, mortgaged, subdivided or cleanly sold, siblings fight, and the deceased's SACCO deposits, coop shares, insurance and pension sit unclaimed. The real blocker is coordinating 8 to 20 relatives to sign, not the court.
ideas.solution: Wedge product is a 'Family Estate Map' for roughly KES 15-25k (pricing to be tested). The child sends photos of the title, IDs, death certificate and old share certificates over WhatsApp. An LLM pipeline extracts names and parcel numbers, handles the multiple-name and spelling-variant problem in Kenyan naming, builds the family tree and likely heirs, and lists the consents needed. It runs official land searches and asset-discovery letters to SACCOs, coops, insurers and the Unclaimed Financial Assets Authority, then outputs a court-ready bundle of forms and affidavits. A home-county field agent collects the chief's letter and relatives' signatures or thumbprints, with video proof of consent. Partner advocates then file and shepherd the case at their own scale fees. Later upsells are surveyor subdivision and lease or loan readiness.
ideas.why_now: The generation that took up land in the 1960s-80s through settlement schemes and land-buying companies is dying now, so the succession backlog is peaking. Diaspora remittances are near record levels (roughly US$5bn a year), and families increasingly ask 'sort out the land' rather than 'build a house'. Digitised land records (Ardhisasa) and court e-filing reduce physical running, though their current coverage needs checking. LLMs can now read messy scanned title and ID documents and draft forms in English while chatting with clients in Swahili. I could not run live searches, so verify current UFAA agent rules, court e-filing scope for successions, and fee schedules before building.
ideas.revenue_model: Flat fee per estate file, paid by M-Pesa or card from abroad. Advocate fees are billed by the advocates themselves, so the company sells software and case management and does not split fees with non-lawyers. Asset discovery is a flat add-on fee, not a percentage cut of UFAA payouts, because UFAA discourages middlemen taking a share. B2B revenue is per cleaned member estate from SACCOs and coops. Later there is referral income from surveyors and land-backed lenders once titles are clean.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Rural Kenya's biggest pool of unused collateral is land trapped in the name of the dead. The bottleneck is family coordination and evidence gathering, so the product is a coordination workflow sold to the sibling who has money and guilt, not a land registry or a lawyer marketplace. VCs looking at land-tech miss that the payer is the diaspora child, not the farmer.
ideas.first_30_days: Pick one county (for example Murang'a or Kakamega) and recruit two advocates who already do succession work. Build intake on WhatsApp Business, Airtable and an LLM extraction script. Sell 10 files at a pilot discount through your own family network, church and alumni groups, and diaspora WhatsApp and Facebook groups such as Kenyans in Texas or the UK. Publish a free 'Is your family land still in a dead man's name?' checker as lead-gen. Track days from intake to gazettement as the core metric.

ideas.title: Fees-in-Kind: Harvest Becomes School Fee Credit
ideas.one_liner: A weigh-in and ledger service that lets parents pay school fees with maize, beans and potatoes at a transparent price, while schools get cheaper, steadier food supply.
ideas.customer: Boards of management, principals and bursars of public boarding and day secondary schools, including the new senior-school cohorts, plus rural private schools. The end users are smallholder parents in maize, bean and potato zones.
ideas.problem: Farm households are asset-rich and cash-poor exactly when fees fall due in January, May and August. Schools already accept 'a tin of maize' informally, but the value is whatever the storekeeper or bursar decides, with no receipts. Meanwhile the same schools buy food through brokers at inflated tender prices, and government capitation often arrives late. Children still get sent home over arrears even when the parents' store is full of grain. Food is often the largest line in a boarding school's budget.
ideas.solution: A Fee Credit Ledger. Farmers deliver graded produce to the school store or a village collection point. A standard weigh ticket (photo of the scale plus a moisture reading) generates an SMS receipt, and the value is credited to the learner's fee account at a published reference price such as NCPB or the county market average, minus a small handling margin. The school gets a weekly reconciliation. On the buying side, the platform, registered as an AGPO-eligible youth or women group (check how each school's procurement committee applies the 30% reservation), bids for school food supply and sources from the same parents. It pools, grades and quality-checks (moisture, aflatoxin spot test). An add-on is hermetic storage bags on credit so parents can deliver later in the term rather than dumping at harvest.
ideas.why_now: The first CBC cohort entered senior school in January 2026, expanding boarding and food demand, and the next cohort arrives in January 2027, so schools are planning Term 1 supply now. Capitation delays keep squeezing school food budgets. Cheap Bluetooth scales, moisture meters and M-Pesa and SMS receipts make a trustworthy weigh ticket trivial. Principals in Kenya talk in tight associations, so one working pilot spreads fast.
ideas.revenue_model: A 4-8% handling margin on food flow: schools pay below their current broker-inclusive price and farmers receive above the broker price. Later a per-learner per-term ledger fee (about KES 50-100). Once the ledger produces credit-quality data, short-term financing of fee arrears or school receivables.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: In every rural ward the school is the largest, most predictable institutional food buyer, and the 'fee arrears list' is a timing and valuation mismatch, not poverty. Fintechs treat barter as embarrassing or informal, but for smallholders paying in maize is the default. What is missing is fair valuation and a ledger everyone trusts. The AGPO set-aside is an under-used entry ticket for farmer groups into school tenders.
ideas.first_30_days: Sign 2-3 principals through your own old high school or a heads' association branch meeting for a one-term pilot in January 2027. Buy two Bluetooth hanging scales and moisture meters (a few hundred dollars), run the ledger on Google Sheets plus Africa's Talking SMS, and recruit 100 parent households at PTA meetings. Set the price at the midpoint between the farmgate broker price and the school tender price. Register the entity for AGPO and open a supplier profile with the school.

ideas.title: Funeral Committee Escrow and Fixed-Price Vendor Network
ideas.one_liner: A per-funeral M-Pesa vault where contributions can only be released to pre-priced vendors with two-of-three committee approvals, ending the 'where did the burial money go' fights.
ideas.customer: The family and burial committee (treasurer, chair, village elder, workplace welfare group) organising a rural funeral, usually with a Nairobi or diaspora fundraising arm. Vendors (tent and chair hire, caterers, coffin makers, embalmers, hearse and PA operators) are the second paying side.
ideas.problem: A rural funeral is often a family's biggest single cash event, drawing hundreds of mourners and costing multiples of a year's farm income. It is run on WhatsApp groups and an exercise book. Treasurer fraud and 'the money vanished' accusations are common and can split families for years. Vendors quote inflated prices to grieving families who cannot shop around, mortuary storage fees accrue daily so decisions are rushed, and families often sell land, borrow against coop shares or take mobile loans to close the gap. Existing crowdfunding tools collect money but do nothing about how it is spent.
ideas.solution: Each funeral gets a dynamic M-Pesa paybill account and a WhatsApp bot (English, Swahili, Sheng). The committee picks from fixed-price packages (basic, standard, large) with vendor prices published. Every payout to a vendor till needs two of three designated approvers by USSD PIN, and a live ledger is visible to all contributors. The bot also handles pledge tracking, reminders in the Nairobi and home committees, the mortuary and transport schedule, and a post-funeral accounting statement. Money sits in a licensed payment provider's trust account, not on the startup's balance sheet.
ideas.why_now: M-Pesa paybill, till and B2B payout APIs are mature enough to make programmable escrow cheap, and the WhatsApp Business API is inexpensive. LLMs now let a bot handle Swahili and Sheng committee chatter. The post-2023 cost-of-living squeeze makes families more sensitive to funeral overspending and to selling land to pay for it. Funeral crowdfunding has trained diaspora and urban Kenyans to give online, but nobody controls the spend side.
ideas.revenue_model: About 2-3% fee on money flowing through the vault plus negotiated vendor margins or referral commissions of roughly 8-12% on vendor spend. Later upsells are funeral cover (partnered with a licensed insurer), memorial pages, and body-transport routing between Nairobi and up-country.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Money that is locked to named vendors is welcome, not resented: it protects the treasurer from the 'sharing tax' of relatives and neighbours asking for cash, and from accusations. In effect the product sells social protection, not payments. Funerals are also where families mortgage their long-term farm assets, so reducing funeral overspend is a farm-resilience product that VCs would never classify as agtech.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 vendors (tents, catering, coffins, hearse) along one corridor such as Nairobi to Murang'a or Nyeri and agree fixed package prices. Onboard the first 5 funerals by offering free setup through church welfare groups, alumni groups and your own contacts, using a manual approval flow on top of an existing paybill provider. Charge the fee only after a funeral closes with a clean statement, and use those statements as proof for the next 50.

ideas.title: Reverse Mzigo: Parents' Farm Feeds Nairobi Kids
ideas.one_liner: A weekly, consolidated truck route that moves food from rural parents' farms to their own adult children in Nairobi estates, paid by the children, turning an informal favour into a subscription that gives parents a dignified monthly income.
ideas.customer: Urban salaried Kenyans (25-45) who already receive 'mzigo' (parcels of maize flour, arrowroot, sweet potatoes, bananas, sukuma, eggs, kienyeji chicken) from their rural mothers. Suppliers are the mothers and other smallholders in their village cluster. Friends and neighbours of the children are the natural second wave of buyers.
ideas.problem: Farm-to-consumer startups keep dying on trust and customer acquisition: urban buyers do not trust unknown farmers and farmers do not trust unknown buyers. Yet a huge informal flow already exists in the opposite direction from the usual assumption: parents send food to their city children by matatu drivers and bus parcel counters, unreliably, unweighed, unrecorded, with spoilage and no payment trail. The children also quietly want to support their parents but handouts hurt parental pride and get 'shared' with relatives.
ideas.solution: Village-cluster pickup and Nairobi last-mile drops, organised by a WhatsApp group per village and a simple order cycle. The child orders or subscribes (say KES 2,000-4,000 per fortnight) and pays by M-Pesa. The parent gets paid the same day on delivery of graded, weighed produce at the village collection point. The platform handles packaging, a consolidated Saturday truck or van, cold-ish handling for chicken and eggs, and a photo receipt with 'from Mama Wanjiku' provenance. Buying food from mum becomes a socially acceptable remittance that preserves her dignity and creates predictable monthly income. Over time it adds friends-of-the-family boxes, bulk orders for church and workplace groups, and inputs credit for the mothers repaid out of box sales.
ideas.why_now: Urban food inflation and food-safety anxiety have pushed Nairobi professionals to look for known-source food. Mobile-money receipts and WhatsApp Business make the order-to-payment loop nearly free to run. Delivery infrastructure (van pooling, boda last-mile) is cheap enough in Nairobi estates to support a weekly consolidated route. Most Nairobi residents keep strong up-country ties, so the founder's own network is a zero-cost acquisition channel.
ideas.revenue_model: Delivery and platform margin of about 12-18% on box value (parents keep roughly 60-70%, transport and packaging the rest), plus a small subscription or priority-delivery fee. Later, inputs and micro-loan referrals to the mothers, and corporate or church bulk orders.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The customer for rural produce is the farmer's own child, not a stranger. Family trust is a free, pre-built distribution network, and it removes the customer acquisition and trust costs that kill farm-to-fork startups. It also means the product is really a disguised remittance channel: paying for goods is a more comfortable way to support parents than sending cash.
ideas.first_30_days: Use your own parents' village and 10 neighbouring mothers, plus 40 Nairobi households from your WhatsApp contacts (school, church, workplace groups). Run one Saturday route on a hired pickup with a Google Form for orders and M-Pesa till for payment. Measure spoilage, on-time rate and how often children reorder, then add a second village once the unit economics on the first route are positive.

ideas.title: Side-Selling Early Warning for Milk and Coffee Coops
ideas.one_liner: A churn-prediction and targeted-advance service that tells dairy and coffee cooperatives which farmers are about to side-sell to cash brokers, and triggers the right cash intervention before the volume walks away.
ideas.customer: Managers and boards of medium-sized dairy cooperatives (about 2,000-10,000 farmers), coffee cooperative societies and factories, and mid-sized processors that buy from farmer groups. They pay because lost throughput hits fixed factory costs and credit recovery.
ideas.problem: Side-selling is the silent killer of Kenyan coops. Farmers sell milk to hawkers and raw-milk traders, or coffee cherry to cash buyers, who pay on the spot, while the coop pays monthly or later and then deducts for feeds, inputs, AI services and loans. Deliveries fade slowly, not suddenly, so managers notice too late. Side-selling spikes when a farmer's net pay is squeezed by deductions, when payment is late, or in cash-crunch weeks such as January and other school fee dates, funerals and sickness. Coops respond with lectures and warnings instead of predicting and fixing the cash gap.
ideas.solution: Ingest the coop's delivery and payment history (usually already exported from the weighing or dairy management software). A simple gradient-boosted or rule-based model scores each farmer weekly for side-selling risk using delivery drift, missed pay days, deductions as a share of gross, days since last payment, seasonality and school-term calendars. The coop gets a daily short list for its field officer, with SMS or voice-call scripts in the local language. The intervention is a coop-funded, capped advance or deduction holiday for at-risk farmers in their predicted cash-crunch window, since the coop already holds the delivered stock and the farmer's record as collateral. It measures recovered litres or kilos against a control group.
ideas.why_now: Global arabica prices spiked to record highs in 2025 and pulled cherry towards cash brokers in Kenya, at the same time as coffee-sector reforms push coops to pay faster and more transparently. Weighing scales and dairy management software have digitised delivery data at many coops over the last five years, so the data now exists. M-Pesa bulk disbursement makes weekly or on-demand advances cheap. Modern ML tooling makes a credible model a two-week job rather than a research project. I could not verify current legal specifics, so confirm the latest coffee and dairy regulations and data-protection obligations (coop as data controller) before pilots.
ideas.revenue_model: Performance fee of roughly 5-10% of recovered volume value (paid from the additional milk or cherry that stays in the coop), or a SaaS retainer of a few tens of thousands of shillings per month per coop. Later, licensing the model to processors and lenders who want a farmer reliability signal.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Side-selling is not disloyalty, it is a rational response to cash-flow timing. The winning intervention is not a scolding letter but a small advance placed at the right moment, funded by the coop's own working capital. It is also predictable from delivery patterns weeks before it happens, because farmers taper deliveries before they stop. Most agritech sells farmers new products, whereas here the buyer is the institution that quietly loses 10% or more of its volume.
ideas.first_30_days: Get 24 months of delivery and payment CSVs from one or two coops, ideally through your own parents' society or the manager you know personally. Build the risk model in a notebook, deliver a top-200 at-risk list plus a script, and run a 60-day test where half the list gets the SMS and advance offer and half does not. Agree to be paid only on retained volume compared to the control group, and use the result as the case study for the next five coops.

ideas.title: Dog Walkers as Repeat-Pass Sidewalk Inspectors
ideas.one_liner: Pay dog walkers a few dollars a day to mount a phone on their chest and sell the resulting block-by-block sidewalk condition layer to cities, utilities, and delivery-robot operators.
ideas.customer: City public works and ADA coordinators (mid-size cities of 100k to 500k people first), plus fiber and utility contractors and sidewalk delivery-robot operators as second buyers. Walkers are the paid supply side.
ideas.problem: Cities are legally on the hook to inventory sidewalks and curb ramps and fix trip hazards. Today that means an expensive contractor van or LiDAR survey every 5 to 10 years, or 311 complaints that skew toward loud, wealthy neighborhoods. Residential side streets go stale, and nobody sees a slab heave, a missing curb ramp, or a new obstruction until someone sues or gets hurt.
ideas.solution: A harness or chest mount plus a background app that runs during walks. It records geotagged video, and an on-device model flags heaved slabs, missing or noncompliant curb ramps, obstructions, standing water, and broken glass. Faces and plates are blurred on the phone and nothing is recorded near windows or interiors. Walkers earn per validated mile (roughly $1 a mile, so about $8 to $15 a day for something they already do). The city gets a rolling map with change detection, exported to its existing GIS or asset-management tools. A free 'dog hazard' layer (glass, bait or poison reports, hot pavement, off-leash aggressive dogs) gives walkers and owners a reason to adopt it. I have not verified current competitors or municipal pricing, so both should be checked before the pitch.
ideas.why_now: In 2026 a phone can run a decent defect-detection model offline, which was not practical a few years ago. Cities face ongoing ADA sidewalk obligations and litigation risk with tight budgets, which favors cheap continuous data over big one-off surveys. Driver-sourced street imagery (Hivemapper and Nexar style) has proven that crowds get paid for mapping, but the pedestrian tier is essentially unclaimed.
ideas.revenue_model: Annual municipal data subscription, or per-mile survey pricing that undercuts contractor quotes, at roughly $20k to $150k a year per city. Secondary sales of the same data to utilities, telecom build QA, and robot-delivery mapping. Walkers are paid about 30 to 40 percent of revenue as per-mile payouts.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: Nobody walks a residential sidewalk more than a dog walker: the same 3 to 5 miles, five days a week, at a slow pace, with eyes on the ground because dogs eat everything. The scarce asset in infrastructure data is not coverage, it is repeat passes, which is what makes change detection possible. That is exactly what a walker's fixed route produces for free.
ideas.first_30_days: Recruit 15 to 20 walkers through local pet-sitter Facebook groups and Nextdoor, since they are already clustered by neighborhood. Build the capture app with a cheap phone mount and an open sidewalk-defect model fine-tuned on public sidewalk datasets. Map about 200 miles of one neighborhood, then take a before-and-after sample to a city ADA or transportation coordinator. Offer a free neighborhood pilot with a cost comparison against contractor rates, and aim for a small pilot purchase order under the city's simple-purchase threshold.

ideas.title: Vet-Prescribed Walks for Post-Surgery and Senior Dogs
ideas.one_liner: Certify dog walkers to deliver vet-written controlled-walking protocols after cruciate and spinal surgery, and to send structured mobility reports back to the clinic.
ideas.customer: Owners of dogs recovering from orthopedic or spinal surgery (TPLO, luxating patella, IVDD) and owners of senior arthritic dogs. Referral partners are surgical and rehab vet practices, who get reports at no charge.
ideas.problem: Discharge sheets say things like '5-minute leash walks four times a day, add 5 minutes a week,' and working owners cannot do it. Dogs get over-exercised or under-exercised and some re-tear the repair, which is a $4k to $6k mistake. Most walkers are afraid of the liability, and most vets don't trust an unspecified walker to follow a protocol. Meanwhile arthritic seniors decline slowly and owners miss it, while the walker sees the hesitation at stairs and the shorter walks first.
ideas.solution: A short walker certification (protocol cards written with two partner rehab vets, sling and non-slip handling, escalation rules). Visits are timed, leash-controlled, and followed by a structured report covering minutes walked, a 0 to 4 gait score, stiffness on rising, toileting, and a 15-second weight-bearing video. The report goes to the owner and the clinic ahead of the 2, 6, and 8 week rechecks. Red flags (swelling, heat, toe-touching) trigger a same-day call. A senior SKU gives a monthly mobility check with a gait video and pain questionnaire, so owner and vet can see whether joint meds or the newer arthritis injectables are actually working.
ideas.why_now: Vets are short-staffed and cannot run rehab follow-ups themselves. Pet insurance adoption keeps growing, so owners protecting a multi-thousand-dollar surgery will pay for compliance. The newer arthritis injectables raised the need for objective at-home response tracking, and safety debates around them make vets want data. Return-to-office pushes more owners out of the house all day right when recoveries need multiple short visits.
ideas.revenue_model: Post-op bundle of roughly $900 to $1,800 over 6 to 8 weeks (short visits at $30 to $45), with the walker keeping about 70 percent. Walker certification fee of roughly $250 to $300. Senior monitoring subscription at about $39 a month. No referral kickbacks to vets, so it stays clean; clinics get the free reports and fewer failed recoveries.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The most valuable clients in this business are not the healthy dogs on the schedule, they are post-op and declining dogs, because the protocol needs several short, geographically tight visits a day and the owner is desperate. The gap is trust, not supply: a protocol and a report format turn 'a walker' into a rehab extender that vets will refer to.
ideas.first_30_days: Sit down with the techs at two local surgical or rehab practices and write a one-page walking progression with them. Get yourself and three walkers through a dry run. Offer the first 10 post-op dogs a reduced bundle in exchange for report feedback, using a simple form that generates a PDF. Ask each clinic to slip a card into TPLO discharge packets and track how many convert.

ideas.title: Paid Shelter-Dog Field Trips, Fees Per Adoption
ideas.one_liner: Professional walkers take the longest-stay shelter dogs on 3-hour public field trips with photos and behavior reports, and shelters pay a small trip fee plus a success fee for each adoption.
ideas.customer: Municipal and county shelters and large humane societies (paying for outcomes), with pet-food brands, pet insurers, and community foundations as sponsors.
ideas.problem: Big adult dogs, especially bully-breed types, sit in kennels for months. Kennel stress makes them look their worst: barking, spinning, lunging. Adopters decide in about 30 seconds. Volunteers do field trips but are untrained for the hard dogs, unreliable, and unscalable. Every extra day in the kennel costs the shelter real money and raises the odds of a bad outcome.
ideas.solution: A walker collects the dog for a 3-hour outing in an 'Adopt Me' vest along a cafe, park, and errand route. They shoot 10 standardized photos and video, and file a behavior report (leash manners, other dogs, cats, car ride, house-training, energy). That content goes onto the shelter's listing and a hyperlocal 'Dog of the Week' list pushed through the walker's client network. Adopted dogs get a paid 7-day decompression check-in that also reduces returns. Everything is tracked against matched dogs to prove the effect on length of stay.
ideas.why_now: Shelters have been running over capacity for the past few years, with intake outpacing adoption and large dogs backing up, and budgets are tight. Housing and landlord pet restrictions keep driving relinquishments. Funders and municipalities increasingly want outcome-based spending, and walkers now have the cheap phone video and social distribution to make a dog look like a dog and not like a kennel number.
