I could not re-verify current national shelter statistics in this session, so quote local data in the pitch.
ideas.revenue_model: About $35 to $50 per field trip paid by the shelter or a sponsor, plus a $150 to $300 success fee per adoption within 30 days. Benchmark the success fee against the shelter's own cost per kennel day. Optional sponsored 'field trip' slots from pet brands and insurers, and grant funding to seed the first shelter.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: A dog is evaluated in the worst possible environment, and the fix is not better marketing, it is moving the evaluation out of the kennel. Professional walkers have exactly what volunteers lack: leash skill with hard dogs, idle midday capacity, and a trusted network of 50 to 100 households that will actually meet a dog because the walker they trust is holding the leash.
ideas.first_30_days: Offer the shelter's volunteer or foster coordinator a free pilot on the 10 longest-stay dogs, with two or three of your own walkers. Track days-to-adoption against similar dogs not taken out. After 30 days, hand the director a one-page results sheet and ask for a paid pilot, or apply for a local pet-industry or community foundation grant to fund the first 100 trips.

ideas.title: Dog Walk Plus: Wellness Checks for Isolated Seniors
ideas.one_liner: Turn the daily dog walk at an older client's home into a consented, structured wellness check with escalation, sold to their adult children.
ideas.customer: Adult children of independent-living parents who own dogs and live alone (the payer). Later: geriatric care managers, home health agencies, senior housing operators, and long-term care insurers.
ideas.problem: A dog walker is the only outsider who enters an older person's home every day at a predictable hour. I have found clients on the floor, and noticed early cognitive decline: the dog fed twice or not at all, pills left out, mail piling up, new bruises. Adult children call and ask us informally, we have no protocol, no consent, and no escalation ladder. Seniors refuse pendants and sensors but accept a walker, because it is about the dog and their dignity stays intact. The dog is also why many seniors delay going to the ER.
ideas.solution: A 'Walk Plus' plan built on a written consent from the senior. Alongside the walk, the walker does a 60-second structured check (a 10-tap list covering mobility, orientation, medications visible, food in the fridge, home temperature, bruises, mood, dog condition). Family gets a weekly text summary with trend flags. There is a clear escalation ladder (no answer at the door, then family call, then agreed non-emergency welfare check), and a pet emergency plan with keys and authority on file so that if the owner is hospitalized the walker becomes the dog's custodian. That prevents surrenders and removes the reason to refuse the hospital.
ideas.why_now: A large cohort is turning 65 and aging in place, home-care aide capacity is tight, and adult children are stretched thin as remote caregivers. Structured notes are now easy to summarize into a plain-language weekly update. Health plans and senior-service providers are looking for cheap ways to catch problems early, and a daily reason to enter the home is exactly what monitoring products lack.
ideas.revenue_model: Walks at $25 to $45 per visit plus a $29 to $49 monthly check-in fee paid by the family. B2B later: license the protocol and reporting to home health agencies and senior housing operators, and sell trend data (with consent) to long-term care insurers or aging-in-place programs.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The dog is the Trojan horse that makes monitoring acceptable. A pendant says 'you're frail'; a dog walker says 'I'm here for the dog.' Walkers already do this informally and unpaid, so the product is less a new service than a protocol, a consent form, and an escalation path around something that already happens every day.
ideas.first_30_days: Convert existing senior clients (most walkers have three to six) with a one-page consent form. Build the check-in with a form and Twilio text summaries, no app needed. Partner with two local geriatric care managers who charge by the hour for the same visibility, and post in senior center and church newsletters. Target 10 paying families and track escalations as your proof.

ideas.title: Guaranteed Midday Walker as Apartment Amenity
ideas.one_liner: Sell apartment operators a fixed on-site walker window as a renewal and lease-up amenity, with residents paying a discounted per-walk fee and the building paying a retainer.
ideas.customer: Owners and property managers of 150 to 500 unit multifamily buildings in dense metros, paying a monthly retainer. Residents are the secondary payers.
ideas.problem: A solo walker loses 35 to 45 percent of the paid day to driving between homes, parking, and building lobbies. Buildings, meanwhile, pay quietly for dogs: barking and noise complaints, damage from anxious dogs, waste on the property, and hidden-dog lease violations. Pet owners renew at higher rates than other tenants, but it is hard to monetize them with pet rent, especially where fees are capped or scrutinized.
ideas.solution: A walker holds fixed weekday windows (for example 11am to 2pm and 5 to 7pm) in the building, using the fob and package room. Residents book by QR code or text, and the walker walks compatible dogs from nearby floors in groups of 3 to 4 (dog compatibility is something a walker learns quickly), with a lobby handoff. Yield per hour roughly doubles or triples versus door-to-door, so residents pay about $12 to $15 per walk instead of $25 to $30. The building gets a monthly report on walks completed, incidents, and waste-bag use, plus marketing copy ('guaranteed midday walk') for lease-up and renewals. I could not confirm in this session whether a comparable product already operates at scale, so check competitors first.
ideas.why_now: Return-to-office mandates put more dogs alone midday. Big multifamily supply waves in many metros mean operators compete on concessions and retention, and are shifting amenity spend from gyms to services. Pet-fee restrictions in some states and cities push operators to bundle services instead of charging rent. Simple text-and-QR booking removes the back-office cost that used to make this unprofitable.
ideas.revenue_model: Building retainer of roughly $1,500 to $3,000 a month for guaranteed windows, plus resident per-walk fees of $12 to $15, plus optional add-ons (waste station servicing, dog-friendly move-in tours). Expand by selling to regional operators as a portfolio amenity program.
ideas.non_obvious_insight: The walker's real margin killer is geography, not demand. A walker's hourly income is decided by drive time and cancellations, so the fix is to put demand where the walker already is. What operators really buy is not walks, it is fewer noise complaints and higher pet-owner renewals, so price it against retention, not against Rover.
ideas.first_30_days: Start with a building where you already walk two or three dogs. Ask those residents to introduce you to the community manager. Pitch a 60-day pilot at about $750 a month with walk windows and a resident-sign-up QR poster. Measure sign-ups and complaints, then take the numbers to two more buildings in the same operator or neighborhood.
